title: Design a natural resource management plan

lessons.title: Inventory and assessment of natural resources
lessons.html:
What a natural resource management plan covers

A natural resource management (NRM) plan sets out how a farm or community will use and protect its soil, water, veld, forests, wetlands, biodiversity and the ecosystem services they provide, such as clean water, pollination and grazing. It links conservation with production, so that resources support the business for generations.

Step 1: define the planning area and stakeholders

The plan may cover one farm, a catchment, a conservancy or communal land. Identify everyone with an interest: owners, workers, communal users, traditional authorities, neighbours, government departments and conservation agencies. Involving them early improves information and support.

Step 2: resource inventory

ResourceWhat to assess
SoilsTypes, depth, erodibility, current erosion, fertility
WaterRivers, dams, boreholes, wetlands, water use rights, quality
Veld and vegetationVeld types, condition, carrying capacity, bush encroachment, alien invasive plants
BiodiversityThreatened species, protected areas, ecological corridors
ClimateRainfall, drought frequency, fire risk
Land useCropland, grazing, infrastructure, settlements

Use aerial photographs, satellite imagery, GIS layers (including provincial biodiversity plans), field surveys and local knowledge.

Step 3: assess condition and threats

Identify degradation and its causes: overgrazing, poorly located roads, invasive plants such as wattle or prosopis consuming water, uncontrolled fires, wetland drainage, pollution. Rank problems by severity and urgency.

Legal context

Relevant laws include the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983, the National Water Act 36 of 1998, the National Environmental Management Act 107 of 1998 and the National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004, which deals with threatened species and invasive species.

lessons.title: Setting goals and choosing management actions
lessons.html:
From problems to plans

Vision and objectives

Write a short vision, for example 'a productive farm with healthy veld, clean rivers and growing wildlife numbers'. Then set SMART objectives: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

  • Increase average ground cover in camps 4 to 9 from 55% to 75% within five years.
  • Clear and follow up 40 ha of wattle along the river within three years.
  • Rehabilitate two dongas before the next rainy season.

Management actions by resource

  • Veld: stocking rates matched to carrying capacity, rotational grazing with rest, fire management plan, bush thinning where encroachment is a problem.
  • Soil: conservation agriculture, contour works, gully rehabilitation, keeping steep land under permanent cover.
  • Water: protect wetlands and riparian buffers, efficient irrigation, pollution prevention, lawful use.
  • Invasive species: integrated control combining mechanical, chemical (registered herbicides as per label) and biological control, with follow-up for several years.
  • Biodiversity: leave corridors, protect habitats of threatened species, manage predators with non-lethal methods first where possible.
  • Fire: firebreaks, fire protection association membership, fire-fighting equipment and trained crews.

Prioritising

Not everything can be done at once. Rank actions by impact, cost, urgency and legal requirement. Protect what is still in good condition first; it is cheaper than restoring degraded land.

Zoning the land

Map land into management zones: intensive production, extensive grazing, conservation areas, rehabilitation sites and buffers. Each zone gets its own rules.

lessons.title: Implementation, monitoring and adaptive management
lessons.html:
Putting the plan to work

Action plan

For each action record what will be done, where, by whom, when, with what resources and at what cost in ZAR. A simple table or Gantt chart helps. Identify funding: farm budget, government programmes such as Working for Water or landcare initiatives, conservation partnerships or carbon and biodiversity schemes where available.

Capacity and people

Train staff in skills such as herbicide application, veld condition assessment and firefighting. Use PPE and safe work procedures under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, especially for chainsaws, herbicides and fire work. Involve communities in decisions and benefits.

Monitoring

  • Fixed-point photographs each season.
  • Veld condition and ground cover assessments.
  • Erosion markers and gully measurements.
  • Water quality and flow measurements.
  • Records of hectares cleared and follow-up done.
  • Species counts for key wildlife or birds.

Adaptive management

Ecosystems are complex and plans rarely work exactly as expected. Adaptive management treats actions as experiments: monitor results, compare with objectives and adjust actions. For example, if ground cover does not improve after two years of rotational grazing, review stocking rate, rest periods or rainfall effects.

Reporting and review

Report progress to owners and stakeholders yearly. Review the full plan every three to five years or after major events such as drought, floods or fires.

Key points

  • Start with a stakeholder-informed inventory of soils, water, veld and biodiversity.
  • Identify degradation and its causes, then set SMART objectives.
  • Prioritise protecting good-condition resources and urgent problems.
  • Zone the land and assign actions, responsibilities and budgets.
  • Monitor and adapt; review the plan regularly.
